statement: In healthy volunteers in randomized crossover driving studies, some benzodiazepine sleeping pills taken at bedtime increase weaving on the road the next day compared with placebo (tested in the morning or afternoon, after one or two nights): after one dose, triazolam increased weaving by a standardized mean difference of 1.45 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.85), more than zopiclone, the comparison drug, in a network meta-analysis (Fornaro et al., 2024, accepted manuscript); in on-road tests summarized in a narrative review, flurazepam and loprazolam at their higher doses impaired driving the next day more than a blood alcohol level of 1.0 g per litre, and nitrazepam, flunitrazepam and lormetazepam at their higher doses about as much as 0.5 to 0.8 g per litre (Vermeeren, 2004, figures second-hand); 0.5 g per litre is the legal driving limit in several countries. Temazepam, flunitrazepam and lormetazepam at the doses in the network did not differ significantly from placebo, but each estimate comes from one small trial and its interval reaches as high as zopiclone's effect. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Some benzodiazepine sleeping pills made healthy volunteers drive worse the next morning, in some studies worse than alcohol at the driving limit used in several countries; for others the studies were too small to tell.
population: Healthy adult volunteers, mostly aged 20 to 65 (one network trial in adults aged 55 to 75), and in some on-road studies women with insomnia who had used sleeping pills before
exposure: A benzodiazepine sleeping pill taken at bedtime, once or for a few nights: triazolam, temazepam, flunitrazepam, lormetazepam, flurazepam, nitrazepam or loprazolam (study doses on the study cards)
comparator: Placebo in the same people (crossover); zopiclone as an active reference drug
outcome: Weaving (standard deviation of lateral position) in on-road or simulated driving the morning after the dose, compared with the weaving produced by known blood alcohol levels

After a few nights, flurazepam 1.65 (0.98 to 2.32). On-road series (second-hand): worse than a blood alcohol level of 1.0 g per litre for flurazepam and loprazolam at higher doses; equal to 0.5 to 0.8 g per litre for nitrazepam, flunitrazepam and lormetazepam at higher doses and flurazepam at the lower dose; no significant effect for lormetazepam at the lower dose, temazepam soft capsules and nitrazepam at the lower dose.

statement: In healthy young men in a sleep laboratory, morning caffeine after a bedtime benzodiazepine sleeping pill (triazolam or flurazepam), compared with a morning placebo after the same pill, was followed by less sleepiness on four sleepiness measures taken together, although on the nap test alone the difference was clear only after the higher flurazepam dose; performance on reaction-time, memory and other tests, and mood, did not differ significantly, in one small randomized double-blind trial with ten men per group (Johnson et al., 1990). statement: In people prescribed benzodiazepine sleeping pills, observational studies summarized second-hand in a narrative review (Vermeeren, 2004) found more injurious road crashes than without them, mostly in the first weeks after a new prescription (odds ratio 6.5, 95% CI 1.9 to 22.5, in the first two weeks, falling to 1.4 in the second month, in one Canadian cohort), but no clear increase for sleeping pills in a UK case-crossover study (odds ratio 1.2, 0.8 to 1.7) or in one study of older drivers (0.9, 0.4 to 2.0), and in another study of drivers over 65 an increase only for longer-acting benzodiazepines in the first week (1.5, 1.0 to 2.0); in older people, a meta-analysis of 40 studies found about 1.5 times the odds of falls with sedatives and sleeping pills, with risks highest in the first weeks of use and higher with larger doses; in nursing homes, falls were more common with any benzodiazepine. These associations may partly reflect why the pills were prescribed (confounding by indication), and the figures are second-hand. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Crashes and falls were more common in people who had just started sleeping pills in some studies, but not in others, and the studies cannot prove the pills caused them.
population: People prescribed benzodiazepine sleeping pills in Canada, the UK and the US (cohort, case-crossover and case-control studies published from the 1970s to about 2002), including adults over 65
exposure: Use of a benzodiazepine sleeping pill, especially in the weeks after a new prescription
comparator: People or periods without such use
outcome: Injurious road crashes; falls and hip fractures in older people
magnitude: Crashes: odds ratio 6.5 (95% CI 1.9 to 22.5) in weeks 1 to 2 and 3.9 (1.9 to 8.3) in weeks 1 to 4 after a new prescription, 1.4 in the second month (Saskatchewan cohort); 1.2 (0.8 to 1.7) for hypnotics in a UK case-crossover study; 1.0 (0.8 to 1.3) for shorter-acting and 1.5 (1.0 to 2.0) for longer-acting benzodiazepines in the first week in drivers over 65; 0.9 (0.4 to 2.0) in another study of older drivers. Falls in older people: pooled odds ratios 1.54 (sedatives and hypnotics) and 1.48 (benzodiazepines) in a meta-analysis of 40 studies; rate ratios 3.0 in week 1, 2.2 in weeks 2 to 4 and 1.3 later in nursing-home residents.

statement: In healthy volunteers and women with insomnia in driving studies, evidence is insufficient to say whether next-morning impairment after benzodiazepine sleeping pills fades over the first week of nightly use: in a network meta-analysis, residual effects seemed to fall with repeated use, which the authors cautiously put down to tolerance, except for flurazepam, which impaired driving after a few nights (standardized mean difference 1.65, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.32) and lormetazepam's estimate after two nights (0.44, -0.23 to 1.10) was no smaller than after one night (0.43) (Fornaro et al., 2024, accepted manuscript); in on-road studies summarized in a narrative review, impairment after flurazepam increased slightly over 7 nights, impairment after nitrazepam did not diminish over a week, and impairment after lormetazepam at its higher dose peaked after 4 nights and then declined (Vermeeren, 2004, second-hand). No study followed people for more than about two weeks. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel 'designer' benzodiazepines; most of the sources also involved opioids or stimulants), evidence is insufficient to say whether any harm reduction service or policy lowers harm. As described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources found up to July 2025, which mapped them without appraising them (Morrison et al., 2025), the approaches studied were drug checking (11 sources), prescribed benzodiazepines as treatment or safer supply (5), policies on scheduling, prescribing and surveillance (9) and approaches for particular groups (10); by the designs listed in the review's table, 17 were quantitative pilot, retrospective, cross-sectional or similar studies, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 a policy analysis, and none was a randomized trial. About half of the drug-checking sources (5 or 6 of 11 by the review's table, editors' count) tested how well drug-checking methods, mostly portable or point-of-care instruments checked against laboratory analysis, detect benzodiazepines: in 59 samples, a portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometer identified 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam was more than 3% of the sample by weight), against 9% with infrared spectroscopy. At one Canadian service, infrared analysis found alprazolam in 33 of 139 samples (23.7%) that people expected to be alprazolam (Xanax), and of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 14 contained other active ingredients only. In a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group (Park et al., 2020, read in full), among 68 of 103 women who sell or trade sex and use opioids in Baltimore, followed up on average 56 days later (one month in the paper's abstract, and in the review) after receiving fentanyl test strips with training, counselling and naloxone, reported using alone fell from 95 to 68 in 100 (among the 59 who used opioids at follow-up; the abstract's 96%, which the review repeats, is a starting figure for all 103 women or for all 68 who completed) and benzodiazepine use from 22 to 7 in 100; but the drug-use questions, benzodiazepines included, covered six months at the start and one month at follow-up (using alone was asked about the past month both times), the counselling and insert card themselves addressed using alone and mixing other drugs with opioids, the women who used no strip also reduced daily opioid use (9 of 11 to 4 of 11), and overdose, the study's main planned outcome, did not change significantly (6 to 1 women). In an observational study of 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in three US states, followed for 28 days in 2023 (Gelberg et al., 2025, read in full), a fentanyl test-strip result showing fentanyl, compared with one not showing it, went with more reports of using less, taking turns and using near someone who had naloxone. For the amount people reported using, the paper's largest printed odds ratio (for reporting a smaller rather than a larger amount) is for drugs that included illicit benzodiazepines (19.9, against 2.2 for opioids alone). The odds ratio and the table's modelled probabilities do not match the calculation described in the Methods when the same model and covariate weights are used. The model or code is needed to explain the gap, so the probabilities cannot identify a corrected odds ratio or a new ordering of the drug groups; after a result not showing fentanyl on drugs that included benzodiazepines, using more was reported in a modelled 66 in 100 cases (95% CI 9 to 97; 37 in 100 for opioids alone), and the paper gives neither the number of people or tests behind these subgroup estimates nor any adjustment for multiple comparisons. The fold reductions that the paper's abstract, and the review's table, give are the printed odds ratios, not measured falls in the amount used; the study relates self-reported results to self-reported behaviour, analyses no harm or overdose outcome (overdose in the 30 days before the start is only adjusted for) and does not compare people offered drug checking with people who were not, and the review's text words this association as an effect. Prescribed benzodiazepines were described for 6 of 77 residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, whose programme as a whole reported no overdoses (an evaluation the review cites as a preprint), and for more than 70 people experiencing homelessness in Dublin, from whom no feedback was collected; in one inner-London general practice, opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines (127 of 278) stayed in treatment longer than those prescribed none or only briefly (72 months against 34 and 51) and had a lower death rate in treatment than those prescribed none (1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years; the review's table says the occasionally prescribed group had the lowest in-treatment death rate, without a figure), but a larger rise in deaths after leaving treatment, by figures the review reports inconsistently. After Australia moved alprazolam to a stricter schedule in 2014, four of five evaluations summarized in a 2021 review reported large falls in alprazolam use, along with falls in prescribing, dispensing, overdose deaths and poison-centre calls, while figures the authors cite from a letter, without definitions, show benzodiazepine overdose deaths overall rising from 160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015. After the United Kingdom rescheduled temazepam gel capsules, 100 people with long-term use of several drugs, in a qualitative study, described less injecting of capsules but continued injecting of tablets, higher prices, more acquisitive crime and substitution with flunitrazepam. The authors call drug checking the most widely reported approach, with consistently positive outcomes, and the results of prescribing and policy approaches mixed, without having appraised any source; they find harm reduction largely missing for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment, and note that their search, built on the term harm reduction, may have missed studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules have all been tried for people who use benzos, but none has been tested in a way that shows whether it lowers harm. The review's authors call drug checking's results consistently positive, but those results are mostly about what tests detected and what people said they did afterwards. At one checking service, infrared testing found alprazolam, the drug in Xanax, in about 1 in 4 samples people thought were Xanax, and some testing methods often missed 'designer' benzos.
population: People who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel), in 35 sources gathered by one scoping review, most of which also involved opioids or stimulants: drug samples at checking services, clients of harm reduction services, women who do sex work, residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, people in treatment, emergency-department and festival patients, forum posters and poison-centre callers
exposure: Harm reduction services and policies: drug checking, prescribed benzodiazepines (agonist treatment or safer supply), rescheduling, prescribing rules, toxicosurveillance and a poison-centre line
comparator: Mostly none; a few observational comparisons (patients maintained on benzodiazepines against others; positive against negative test results), before-and-after measurements without a control group, and one detection method against another (mostly portable or point-of-care methods against laboratory analysis)
outcome: Detection of benzodiazepines in drug samples; reported behaviour after testing; treatment retention and mortality; prescribing, use and deaths after policy changes; people's accounts
magnitude: No pooled estimates. Detection: portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry 36% of etizolam-containing samples (78% above 3% by weight) against 9% with infrared (59 samples); a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples that strips and/or infrared had failed to detect or quantify. Expected alprazolam: 33 of 139 (23.7%) by infrared; of 20 confirmed, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other ingredients, 14 other ingredients only. Toronto: of 555 samples, 15 were expected to be benzodiazepines, and benzodiazepine-type drugs were found in 116; benzodiazepine-type drugs present in 24 (41%) of samples linked to a negative effect (presence, not cause). After test strips (pilot, 68 of 103 followed up on average 56 days later, called one month in the paper's abstract; Park et al., read in full): using alone 94.9% to 67.8% (n = 59; the abstract's 96% is 96.1% of all 103 or 95.6% of the 68 at the start), benzodiazepine use 22.1% to 7.4%, the drug-use window six months at the start and one month at follow-up (using alone and overdose: past month both times); daily opioid use among the 11 women who used no strip 81.8% to 36.4% (9 to 4); overdose in the past month 6 to 1 women, not significant. Test-strip results and later behaviour (541 adults, 28 days, observational; Gelberg et al., read in full): proportional-odds ratio for reporting a smaller rather than a larger amount, positive against negative result, as printed: 4.37 (3.45 to 5.55) overall, 19.92 (8.57 to 46.27) for illicit benzodiazepines, 10.04 for stimulants only, 4.21 for opioids and stimulants, 2.18 for opioids only, 2.11 for other or unknown drugs; direct cumulative odds ratios calculated from the printed benzodiazepine probabilities are 3.64 and 5.29 (editors' calculations, not replacement adjusted estimates). Allowing rounding to three decimals gives disjoint ranges of 3.39 to 3.92 and 5.26 to 5.31, so no single corrected common odds ratio follows. The stated inverse-link-of-least-squares-mean calculation, using the same model and covariate weights for both results, does not reconcile the printed values; the actual fitted model and prediction code are not supplied; modelled probability of using more after a negative result 0.657 (0.091 to 0.973; benzodiazepines), 0.531 (stimulants only), 0.373 (opioids only), 0.225 overall; after a positive result, overall, less or none 0.090, same 0.847, more 0.063; number of people or tests per drug group not given. Prescribed benzodiazepines: 6 of 77 hotel residents (cited from a preprint); more than 70 people in Dublin. Opioid substitution case notes: retention 72 against 34 and 51 months; in-treatment mortality 1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years (against those prescribed none; lowest in the occasionally prescribed group, no figure given); post-treatment rate in the maintained group 5.90 per 100 years, reported as a 450% rise (4.5 times the in-treatment rate, an increase of about 350%, editors' calculation). Alprazolam rescheduling: 4 of 5 evaluations reported large declines in use; alprazolam-related deaths 57 (2012) to 23 (2015); benzodiazepine overdose deaths 160 (2009) to 238 (2015). Kentucky 'no benzodiazepine' formulary: prescriptions down 89% over two years. Victoria emergency departments, 2020 to 2022: novel benzodiazepine-type drugs in 183 of 1112 drug-toxicity presentations (16.5%). Poison-centre line: safety information to 6635 of 17,616 callers (37.7%), no outcome evaluation.

statement: In older adults (people aged over 66 in Quebec, Canada, in 2000–2009, and people aged 65 or over in the Seattle area, USA, followed between 1994 and 2012), evidence is insufficient to say whether using benzodiazepines (prescribed sedatives such as diazepam, lorazepam, temazepam, clonazepam and triazolam) causes dementia, and the two studies read disagree on whether heavier use goes with more of it. In a case-control study in the Quebec public drug plan's claims database (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014; funded by French public research bodies and the Quebec health research fund), 894 of 1,796 people with a first physician's claims diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (49.8%) and 2,873 of 7,184 controls matched on sex, age group and length of follow-up (40.0%) had filled at least one benzodiazepine prescription 5 to 10 years before the diagnosis date (adjusted odds ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.36 to 1.69; 1.43, 1.28 to 1.60, after also adjusting for recorded anxiety, depression and insomnia). The odds ratio rose with the cumulative amount filled: 1.09 (0.92 to 1.28) for up to about 3 months' supply, 1.32 (1.01 to 1.74) for 3 to 6 months (1.28, 0.97 to 1.69, in the fuller model) and 1.84 (1.62 to 2.08) for more than 6 months (32.9% of cases against 21.8% of controls; 1.74, 1.53 to 1.98, in the fuller model), and was higher for long-acting (1.70) than for short-acting drugs (1.43); counting only prescriptions 6 to 10 years before gave similar results (more than 6 months: 1.79, 1.58 to 2.04). The database holds no information on education, socioeconomic status, smoking or alcohol; the main reasons for prescribing were recorded as diagnoses for far fewer people than filled prescriptions (anxiety in 21.4% of cases and 15.1% of controls, depression in 2.9% and 2.4%, insomnia in 4.0% and 3.2%); and a case-control study gives no absolute risk, nor does this one report any. Its authors acknowledge that benzodiazepine use might be an early marker of a condition that raises dementia risk rather than its cause. In a prospective cohort of 3,434 health-plan members without dementia at entry (Adult Changes in Thought study; Gray et al., 2016; funded by the US National Institute on Aging and the Branta Foundation, which had no role in the study), screened every 2 years and diagnosed by research criteria, 797 (23.2%) developed dementia over a mean of 7.3 years. With pharmacy records summed over a rolling 10-year window that left out the most recent year, crude dementia rates were 30.3 per 1,000 person-years with no use, 36.1 with 1 to 30 standardized daily doses, 39.6 with 31 to 120 and 30.2 with 121 or more (editors' arithmetic, not adjusted for age), and adjusted hazard ratios against no use were 1.25 (1.03 to 1.51), 1.31 (1.00 to 1.71) and 1.07 (0.83 to 1.39, the primary model as printed in the figure; 0.83 to 1.37 in the text and 0.82 to 1.39 in the abstract), with 0.95 (0.71 to 1.27) for Alzheimer's disease at the highest level. The highest level held 267 people at entry and 75 dementia cases in 2,481 person-years, and its median use was 375 standardized daily doses, which the authors equate with slightly over a year of daily use. When the last 2 years of prescriptions were left out, the low-use excess was no longer significant (1.18, 0.97 to 1.44), and in a post hoc analysis leaving out the last 5 years no level was significantly associated with dementia (1.21, 0.98 to 1.50; 1.20, 0.88 to 1.64; 1.13, 0.85 to 1.52); cognitive decline did not differ significantly by use. The cohort's authors write that their interval for the highest level excludes an association as large as the Quebec study's but not a moderate one, that people susceptible to the drugs may have stopped early, a limitation they say other studies share, and that the most susceptible may have developed dementia before they could enrol, which could bias the results towards no association, and that they could not adjust for anxiety or insomnia. Both teams state that anxiety, insomnia and depression, for which benzodiazepines are prescribed, can come in the years before a dementia diagnosis, so prescriptions may follow early dementia rather than cause it (reverse causation); neither study assigned benzodiazepines at random, and neither design can rule this out. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Whether benzodiazepines (prescribed sedatives such as diazepam or lorazepam) cause dementia is not known, and the two studies read disagree. In Quebec health-insurance records, about 50 in 100 older people later diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years before, against 40 in 100 people of the same age and sex without it, and the link was clearest with more than 6 months' supply; but the records held nothing on education, smoking or drinking, often missed why the pills were taken, and cannot give anyone's risk. In a Seattle study that tested 3,434 people aged 65 or over every 2 years, about 3 in 100 a year were diagnosed with dementia among those who had used benzodiazepines most, the same as among those who had used none (before allowing for age); a small extra risk at light or moderate use was no longer clear when the most recent prescriptions were left out, which fits early symptoms of dementia, such as anxiety and poor sleep, leading to prescriptions. That study had few people with heavy use, may have counted people who stopped early among those with little or no use, and could not count people who developed dementia before joining, so a moderate effect is not ruled out.

evidence.locator: Methods › Study design and setting; Selection of cases and controls; Exposure assessment; Potential confounders; Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Case-control study among people aged over 66 living in the community in Quebec, Canada, who were members of the public drug plan from 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2009 (the plan covers about 98% of older Quebec residents), using the provincial administrative claims database (RAMQ): random samples of 38,741 people with a diagnosis or treatment related to dementia (source of cases) and 86,259 without (source of controls). Cases: a first recorded diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (ICD-9 331.0; its date the index date), no earlier record of another dementia, no anti-dementia treatment before it and at least six years of follow-up before it; each matched to four controls on sex, age group (70–74, 75–79, 80–84, 85 or over) and length of follow-up (6 to 10 years) by incidence density sampling. Exposure: pharmacy dispensing claims for all reimbursed benzodiazepines; treatments started less than five years before the index date were not counted, because they could carry reverse-causation bias, so exposure was taken from the window 5 to 10 years before. Ever use meant at least one claim in the window; the cumulative amount was converted to prescribed daily doses (one equals an average day's use in the source cohort): 1 to 90 (up to 3 months), 91 to 180 (3 to 6 months) and more than 180 (over 6 months, long-term use); half-life under 20 hours or 20 hours or more; people with no claim in the window were the reference group. Sensitivity analysis: index date moved back a year (window 6 to 10 years). Covariates from claims in the same window: high blood pressure, myocardial infarction, stroke, platelet inhibitors or oral anticoagulants, high cholesterol, diabetes, a comorbidity indicator, and anxiety, depression and insomnia diagnoses; the last three were left out of the first model because whether they are risk factors or early signs (prodromes) of dementia is debated and their expected strong correlation with benzodiazepine use could lead to overadjustment, and were added in a second model if they did not interact with exposure; conditional logistic regression.

risk_of_bias.note: For the causal question, neither study controls the reasons for prescribing or the symptoms that precede dementia. Case-control study (card sc_billioti_de_gage_2014, ROBINS-E, high): no education, socioeconomic status, smoking or alcohol; anxiety, depression and insomnia known only from claims diagnoses recorded for far fewer people than filled prescriptions; outcome from physicians' claims diagnoses, possibly recorded late and more readily in people seen more often; a reference group that includes anyone who started only in the last 5 years. Cohort (card sc_gray_2016, ROBINS-E, some concerns): people with any earlier use rather than people starting treatment, so those who stopped early after side effects or developed dementia before enrolment are missing from the higher levels (the authors say the second could bias towards no association); anxiety and insomnia not adjusted for; covariates measured at entry, in some cases after exposure began; 614 participants without a follow-up visit excluded and not described. Down one level; not twice for the same problems under inconsistency.

inconsistency.note: The two studies disagree on heavier use: odds ratio 1.84 (1.62 to 2.08) for more than 6 months' supply in Quebec against hazard ratio 1.07 (0.83 to 1.39) at the highest level in Seattle, intervals that do not overlap. The explanations offered (claims-based against research diagnosis, different lags, people with earlier use rather than people starting treatment, possibly lower exposure in Seattle) are untested, and the exposure scales differ (prescribed daily doses at average use against minimum effective doses for older adults).

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for older adults in these two places and periods and for dispensed prescriptions; younger adults were not studied, as the debate box says.

imprecision.note: Not rated down separately: both studies are large; the cohort's highest level is small (267 people at entry, 75 cases) and its interval reaches 1.39, which the statement reports and which is part of why the two answers cannot be reconciled (counted under inconsistency).

large_effect.note: No odds or hazard ratio in the main analyses reaches 2; the 2.51 among people who had stopped at least a year before diagnosis is a subgroup estimate from one study.

dose_response.note: The Quebec gradient by cumulative amount is not used to rate up: its middle step loses significance in the fuller model, longer prescribing could also track longer-lasting anxiety or sleep problems, and the Seattle cohort found no gradient (highest level 1.07; spline back towards 1.0 above about 90 standardized daily doses).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level for risk of bias and one for inconsistency: very low, the floor. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the association in Quebec claims data and the absence of a detectable association at the highest level in the Seattle cohort are reported in it, not rated as separate claims. Status contested (METHODS §6.4, §7): two designs give two answers on heavier use, and reverse causation, early symptoms of dementia leading to prescriptions, is acknowledged by both teams and settled by neither: the Quebec study left out the 5 years before diagnosis, the Seattle cohort the year before each point of follow-up (2 and 5 years in sensitivity analyses). The two samples share no data; the cohort's post hoc five-year lag copies the Quebec method, so the disagreement does not come from the lag alone. No absolute risk can be given from the case-control study; the cohort's crude rates are editors' arithmetic, not adjusted for age, and its adjusted hazard ratios are the comparison that counts. Earlier studies that each paper describes (a French cohort with a positive association, a UK records study without one) have not been read and are not counted. Benzodiazepines are prescribed medicines: the answer reports what the studies found and gives no advice on taking, stopping or reducing them.

debate.question: Does using benzodiazepines cause dementia, as the finding of more past use, and especially more long use, among older people later diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in Quebec claims data suggests to its authors (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014), or do the prescriptions follow early symptoms of dementia, as the authors of a Seattle cohort that found no association at its highest level of use conclude (Gray et al., 2016)?
debate.evidence_yes: In Quebec claims data, people with a first diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease had more often filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years earlier than matched controls (49.8% against 40.0%; adjusted odds ratio 1.51, 1.36 to 1.69); the odds ratio rose with the cumulative amount filled, from 1.09 (0.92 to 1.28) for up to about 3 months' supply to 1.84 (1.62 to 2.08) for more than 6 months, and was higher for long-acting drugs (1.70 against 1.43); adjusting for recorded anxiety, depression and insomnia changed it little (1.43 for any use, 1.74 for more than 6 months), no significant interaction with any of the three was found, and leaving out the 6 years before diagnosis gave similar results (1.79 for more than 6 months) (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014). The authors argue that the 5-year gap makes prescribing for early symptoms less likely, that the gradient with cumulative amount points to a drug effect, and that it seems unlikely that the drugs' effects on thinking confounded the diagnosis, because the odds ratio for more than 6 months' use was 2.51 (1.97 to 3.20) in people who had stopped at least a year before diagnosis and 1.72 (1.51 to 1.97) in people still taking them, subgroup estimates printed without counts or a stated model (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014). In the Seattle cohort, dementia was slightly more frequent with low and moderate cumulative use (hazard ratios 1.25, 1.03 to 1.51, and 1.31, 1.00 to 1.71), and its authors write that they cannot rule out a moderate association at the highest level, whose interval reaches 1.39, and that people susceptible to the drugs may have stopped early, a limitation they say other studies share, and that the most susceptible may have developed dementia before they could enrol, which could bias their results towards no association (Gray et al., 2016). The Quebec authors call five earlier studies congruent, though they say prescribing for early symptoms could not be ruled out in four of them; the fifth is their own French cohort, in which new use went with dementia (hazard ratio 1.62, 1.08 to 2.43, as the Seattle authors report it) (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2016); those studies have not been read here.
debate.evidence_no: In the Seattle cohort, in which everyone was screened every 2 years and dementia was diagnosed by research criteria, the highest cumulative use was not associated with dementia (hazard ratio 1.07, 0.83 to 1.39) or Alzheimer's disease (0.95, 0.71 to 1.27); splitting it gave 1.11 (0.78 to 1.58) and 1.03 (0.73 to 1.44); a continuous model showed the hazard ratio falling back towards 1.0 above about 90 standardized daily doses; cognitive decline did not differ significantly; and crude dementia rates were 30.2 per 1,000 person-years at the highest level and 30.3 with no use (editors' arithmetic) (Gray et al., 2016). The small excess appeared at low and moderate use rather than at the highest, a pattern the authors read as prescribing for early (prodromal) symptoms; the low-use excess lost significance when the last 2 years of prescriptions were left out (1.18, 0.97 to 1.44), and with a 5-year gap like the Quebec study's no level was significantly associated (1.13, 0.85 to 1.52, at the highest) (Gray et al., 2016). The authors note that the interval for the highest level excludes an association of the size reported in Quebec, and attribute the difference mainly to the Quebec study's claims-based diagnosis, which could be late and differentially misclassified, since people with heavy benzodiazepine use may be in contact with health care more often (Gray et al., 2016). The Quebec authors themselves state that anxiety and sleep problems, the main reasons for prescribing, could go with early brain changes of Alzheimer's disease, so that use might mark a condition that raises dementia risk rather than cause it; their database recorded no education, socioeconomic status, smoking or alcohol, and anxiety, depression and insomnia were recorded as diagnoses for far fewer people than filled prescriptions (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014). The Seattle authors describe a UK records study in which high use was not associated with Alzheimer's disease once use begun in the prodromal phase was accounted for (Gray et al., 2016); it has not been read here.
debate.neither_can_show: Neither study assigned benzodiazepines at random, and both measured what pharmacies dispensed, not what people took (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2016). Neither can separate an effect of the drugs from the anxiety, sleep problems and depression they are prescribed for, which become more frequent in the years before a dementia diagnosis and may begin earlier than either study's gap (5 years in Quebec; 1 year, and 2 and 5 years in sensitivity analyses, in Seattle) (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2016). The case-control design gives no absolute risk and relies on claims diagnoses, with the reasons for prescribing missing for most people (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014); the cohort followed people whatever their earlier use, so people who stopped early could not accumulate higher use and those who developed dementia before enrolment could not be counted, it had few people with heavy use, and its participants were mostly white and relatively well educated (Gray et al., 2016). Both studies are of people aged 65 or over and say nothing about younger adults (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2016).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Older people later diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in Quebec claims data had filled more benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years earlier, most clearly with more than 6 months' supply (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014), but a cohort with research diagnoses found no detectable association at its highest level of use, with an interval that excludes the Quebec estimate, and a small excess only at lower levels, as would be expected if early symptoms led to prescriptions (Gray et al., 2016). The disagreement may come from how dementia was diagnosed, from how much and for how long people used the drugs, or from which people each design could include, and none of these has been tested (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2016). The evidence read cannot say whether benzodiazepines cause dementia. It can say that the link seen in claims data was not found with research-standard diagnosis at the levels of use seen in Seattle (median slightly over a year of daily use at the highest level), while a moderate effect at those levels, and any effect of heavier or longer use, remain possible (Gray et al., 2016). This answer reports what the studies found; it gives no advice on taking, stopping or reducing benzodiazepines, which are prescribed medicines.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A cohort comparing people who start a benzodiazepine with people who start another treatment for the same anxiety or sleep problem, with research-standard dementia diagnosis, prescriptions recorded 10 or more years before diagnosis, anxiety, sleep problems, education and alcohol measured, enough people with several years of continuous use, and absolute risks reported, would address the reverse causation and confounding that neither design read here could (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2016); the Quebec authors also call for follow-up of 20 to 30 years to study long-term use in younger adults and the role of anxiety, sleep problems and depression as early risk factors (Billioti de Gage et al., 2014).

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything they do themselves before or during use lowers harm: as described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources that did not appraise them (Morrison et al., 2025), no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm as an outcome of a practice. Practices appear as people's accounts, researchers' recommendations and reports of behaviour after drug checking: in a study of a Swedish online drug forum about flubromazolam (122 in the review's table), posters described limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, in a qualitative study) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in an ethnography in Melbourne, one participant described using temazepam at home to avoid losing money or drugs, or being arrested, while sedated; and the authors of a survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok called for education against injecting alone. Numbers come only from two drug-checking studies, and they describe behaviour, not harm: in a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, in which 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore received fentanyl test strips, 69% of the 68 followed up a month later reported doing something to lower harm after a result, such as asking someone to check on them, and reported using alone fell from 96% to 68%; and in an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went, over 28 days, with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (an association in the review's table, which its text words as a result of the strip). The review searched on terms such as harm reduction and did not cover peer-led resources, so practices described elsewhere may be missing; its authors find harm reduction largely absent for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People who use benzos describe staying at home, keeping the drug out of reach while high, avoiding alcohol at the same time and having friends check on them. In two studies of fentanyl test strips, people said they took more care after a positive result, such as having someone check on them, but harm was not measured. No study found by a 2025 review compared people who do these things with people who do not, so it is not known whether any of them lowers harm.
population: People who use benzodiazepines, including novel ones, in forum, qualitative, ethnographic, survey, pilot and observational sources gathered by one scoping review: posters on a Swedish drug forum; 45 women and gender-diverse people who use drugs in British Columbia; one participant in Melbourne; 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok; 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore; 541 adults who use drugs in several US states
exposure: Practices people use themselves before or during use, as described: limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they use, avoiding alcohol at the same time, comparing vendors and batches, peer check-ins, not using or injecting alone; and reported behaviour after a test-strip result (asking someone to check on them, using smaller amounts, taking turns, keeping naloxone nearby)
comparator: None: no source compared people using a practice with people not using it; the two test-strip studies compared reports before and after receiving strips, or related behaviour to the strip result
outcome: Any harm, such as overdose, assault, injury or arrest (not measured against a comparison in any source); reported behaviour after a test-strip result
magnitude: No source compared people who used a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm. Behaviour after test strips: in a before-and-after pilot (68 of 103 followed up at one month, no control group), reported using alone was 96% before and 68% after, and 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour after a result; in an observational study of 541 adults over 28 days, a positive result went with using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (sizes given only in the review's table, second-hand).

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say how often stopping benzodiazepines suddenly leads to seizures or other severe withdrawal reactions, or how much stopping gradually lowers that risk. As described second-hand in two narrative reviews (Lader, 2011, a descriptive review based on a lecture; Brett & Murnion, 2015, a four-page clinical review for prescribers that cites the 2011 review elsewhere), stopping or cutting down after regular use can bring a withdrawal syndrome: the 2011 review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use but only in about 15 to 30 in 100 patients, a figure cited to the author's own 1998 paper on stopping sleeping pills, and that rebound (the original symptoms returning more strongly for a while) is likely when stopping sleeping pills, especially short-acting ones, even after a few nights of use; the 2015 review states, without a reference, that anyone who has taken a benzodiazepine for longer than 3 to 4 weeks is likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly. Symptoms listed include anxiety and panic, poor sleep and nightmares, poor memory and concentration, low mood, muscle spasms and aches, numbness and tingling, sweating, and heightened sensitivity to light, sound and touch, with feelings of unreality; the 2011 review says they generally fade within weeks or months, often fluctuating, and both reviews say they can resemble the anxiety or insomnia the drug was taken for. Both reviews describe seizures. The 2011 review lists convulsions (which, it says, may end in death), delirium, psychosis, depression, often severe, and suicidal thoughts among reactions that may follow abrupt stopping but may also occur despite slow tapering, with no frequencies, in a table sourced mainly to a university guide and the author's 1984 monograph (the depression entry to a report of four cases), says many of them are reported anecdotally, with few case series, and that their status remains controversial; it adds that whether withdrawal occurs is related to high doses and long treatment but its severity less closely, and that severe withdrawal may occur despite withdrawal over months or years. The 2015 review states, without a reference or a frequency, that abrupt stopping after 1 to 6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures, lists grand mal seizures 1 to 12 days after stopping in a box without a source, and describes people without a history of seizures, unstable medical or psychiatric illness or other drug dependence as at lower risk of harm from withdrawal, also without references. The only count of seizures in either review comes from a 1961 study in which 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months were switched to a dummy pill: within 2 to 8 days, 10 developed withdrawal reactions, including depression, psychosis and agitation, and 2 had seizures. Neither review cites a study comparing sudden with gradual stopping for seizures; the 2011 review says the rate at which doses are reduced rests on prescribers' clinical experience rather than good evidence, and that, in high-dose use as in low-dose dependence, withdrawal can sometimes be severe, with fits and psychotic reactions. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Is it dangerous to stop benzos suddenly? It can be, but the two expert reviews read here, which are not new studies, don't say how often. They describe withdrawal after regular use. One says symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use in about 15 to 30 in 100 people, a figure from the author's own earlier paper, and that sleeping pills can bring back worse sleep for a while even after a few nights. Symptoms include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound, and they can feel like the problem the pills were taken for. Both reviews warn that stopping suddenly can bring seizures that can be life-threatening. But one says most reports of severe reactions are anecdotes, and that they can happen even with slow tapering; the other gives no source for its seizure warning; and neither gives a rate. The only count is from 1961: 2 of 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months had seizures after being switched to a dummy pill.
population: People stopping or reducing regular benzodiazepine use (prescribed anxiolytics and sleeping pills, and high-dose use outside medical care), as described in two narrative reviews; in the one study with a seizure count (1961, as described), 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months
exposure: Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly, or reducing or stopping them gradually, after regular use
comparator: None in the sources described; neither review cites a study comparing abrupt with gradual stopping
outcome: Withdrawal symptoms (how often, which, how long), rebound, and severe reactions including seizures, delirium, psychosis and suicidal thoughts
magnitude: Not estimable for seizures or other severe reactions: neither review gives a frequency. As described: withdrawal symptoms after 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients (Lader, 2011, citing Lader, 1998, ref. 124). 1961 study (Hollister et al., as described): 11 prisoners, chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months, switched to placebo; 10 had withdrawal reactions within 2–8 days and 2 had seizures. The seizure statements in Brett & Murnion (2015) carry no references.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether designer benzodiazepines (benzodiazepines and close relatives sold on the illicit market, such as etizolam, clonazolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam, of which etizolam and phenazepam are licensed medicines in a few countries) are more dangerous than prescribed benzodiazepines: no source read here compares them, and neither source counts the people who used them without coming to attention, so neither gives a risk per use. In US poison-centre records (the National Poison Data System), 474 exposures to designer benzodiazepines were reported from 2014 to 2017; the 234 intentional exposures to one of 11 coded designer benzodiazepines and no other substance were analysed, while the reports involving other substances, about half, were neither collected nor analysed (Carpenter et al., 2019). The 234 were mostly etizolam (162) and clonazolam (50); the median age was 25, 86% were men, and 42 (18 in 100) were coded as suspected suicide. statement: In laboratory studies in which adults first sampled a benzodiazepine and a dummy pill (placebo) and then chose which to take, a history of problem drug use (the papers' 'drug abuse') is associated with choosing the benzodiazepine: volunteers without such a history mostly chose the placebo, and diazepam calmed and sedated them without raising euphoria scores, while people with such a history almost always chose the benzodiazepine, though they were tested in separate studies by another laboratory, mostly at much higher doses, so their history and the dose cannot be told apart. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (each kind of person was studied mainly by one laboratory, and no study read compared people with and without such a history at the same doses). In the one primary study read (de Wit et al., 1986, University of Chicago), 36 paid volunteers aged 21 to 35, recruited through advertisements and posters on a university campus and by word of mouth, told that the study offered money and not treatment, and excluded if they had a history of problem drug use, major depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia (12 without anxiety, 11 with anxious mood and 13 with generalized anxiety disorder; 6 others did not finish, one of them because of diazepam's sedative effects), each took part in three experiments in counterbalanced order: diazepam (Valium) 5 mg, diazepam 10 mg and d,l-amphetamine 5 mg, each against a placebo capsule of another colour (study conditions). They swallowed one capsule between 9 and 10 in the morning and then went about their day; after four sampling sessions they chose which colour to take on five more occasions. Most chose the placebo: at 5 mg, 21 of the 36 chose diazepam at most once and 8 chose it four or five times; at 10 mg, 27 chose it at most once and 5 four or five times (the numbers fell across the choice categories: z = −2.2, P < .03, and z = −3.0, P < .004), whereas 20 of the 36 chose amphetamine four or five times (z = 2.3, P < .02). The anxious groups chose no differently from the others, but with 11 to 13 people a group only large differences could have been seen (editors' note). Among people who liked one capsule better during the sampling sessions, more liked the placebo: 17 against 8 at 5 mg and 21 against 9 at 10 mg (editors' sums from Table 5). Diazepam lowered ratings of anxiety, vigour and arousal and raised ratings of confusion and sedation, 10 mg also raised fatigue, and on 10 mg days depression and dysphoria scores were higher and friendliness, elation and positive mood scores lower than on placebo days; the euphoria scale did not change significantly at either dose, while amphetamine raised it. Most people recognised 10 mg diazepam as a tranquilizer (30 of 36). The volunteers were not new to drugs (29 of the 36 had used marijuana, 19 stimulants and 6 tranquilizers outside medical care, and 9 drank more than 7 drinks a week; editors' sums from Table 2), but choice was not analysed by drinking or drug history. The authors' conclusion that highly anxious people are not at greater risk of dependence goes beyond what was tested, single morning doses on separate days; they add that people in acute distress, people less bothered by sedation, people expecting a particular effect and people with much earlier sedative or alcohol use might respond differently. A narrative review of laboratory studies published up to 1997, by two authors at Johns Hopkins University (Griffiths & Weerts, 1997; no stated search; its figures are second-hand here, as the primary papers were not read), calls a person's history the most important single factor in whether a benzodiazepine is chosen. In 13 studies of people with 'histories of drug abuse' (2 to 16 people each, men in all but one, 11 of the 13 co-authored by the review's first author; editors' counts from Table 2 and the reference list), the benzodiazepine was almost always chosen, or taken more than its comparison: for example, 16 men chose diazepam over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% of occasions; but four of the 13 studies had no placebo comparison (editors' count), triazolam was taken more than placebo by 4 of 6 men in one study, and in another all 8 men chose triazolam before a relaxation task and none before a vigilance task. In 17 studies of people without such histories (12 with de Wit or Johanson of the Chicago group among the authors; editors' count), healthy volunteers who were light drinkers without anxiety or insomnia consistently did not choose a benzodiazepine over placebo (for example diazepam on 25% to 38% of choice sessions in four studies, lorazepam on 16% and flurazepam on 20%), in several studies choosing it significantly less often than placebo, while amphetamine was chosen under similar conditions. Most of the studies in people with histories of problem drug use gave much higher doses (for example diazepam 40 to 400 mg in three of them, against diazepam in single doses of 2 to 20 mg or in 4 mg capsules taken one at a time in the studies of other volunteers; study conditions), and the review itself reports that choice depended on dose, yet it does not discuss dose as an explanation of the difference between the two kinds of people (editors' reading). What the review counts as a drug being chosen for its effects (reinforcement) covers any reason, whether to feel good, to ease anxiety or to avoid withdrawal, so choosing a benzodiazepine does not by itself show that people felt high. Moderate social drinkers (about 12 drinks a week) chose diazepam over placebo in three studies, on 100%, 73% and 64% of choices, while light drinkers (about 4 a week), tested under the same procedure in two of them, did not significantly prefer it (66%, a non-significant tendency, and 40%; the difference from moderate drinkers significant in the second); the moderate drinkers more often used marijuana weekly, and the review says that people with a history of moderate drinking or of alcoholism showed greater positive mood effects from benzodiazepines (no figures given), while calling what the drinkers' preference means for real-life risk unclear. In anxious people the results were mixed and lined up with how the drug was offered: two studies with a single morning dose found no preference (de Wit et al., 1986, and 14 people seeking treatment, who chose diazepam on 37% of sessions), while three that let people decide when and how many capsules to take found one (65% of evening sessions in 22 anxious volunteers against 45% in 23 volunteers without anxiety, P = 0.06; 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder, and 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder, taking capsules as needed over 4 weeks, mostly at low, stable rates). People with insomnia chose triazolam on 86% of nights when they had to pick it or a placebo at bedtime, but took placebo capsules as often as triazolam when either was simply on offer. The review flags its comparisons across studies as not tested prospectively. As cited by the review, about half of US high-school students who reported non-medical use of tranquilizers (mostly benzodiazepines) said they usually got high from them (a survey report covering 1975 to 1992, with no single year given). In a US national survey of 2015 and 2016, getting high was the main reason given by 11.6% of adults who reported misusing benzodiazepines, behind relaxing and sleep (see the answer on why people misuse benzodiazepines). The laboratory studies date from 1976 to 1997, are small, used capsules prepared by the researchers, and none that the review describes followed whether choosing a benzodiazepine in the laboratory predicts later use outside it.
plain: Do benzos get you high, and who likes them? In lab studies, it depended on who people were. In one study, 36 young volunteers with no history of drug problems, though most had tried cannabis, took diazepam (Valium) or a dummy pill on different mornings and then chose which one to take, five more times. Most chose the dummy pill: at the higher of two doses, 27 of the 36 picked diazepam once at most. It calmed them and made them sleepy and a bit muddled, and it did not raise their euphoria scores; at the higher dose they also felt more tired and less cheerful and friendly than after the dummy pill. Volunteers with anxiety chose it no more often than the others, though it eased their anxiety. A review of older lab studies, whose figures are second-hand here, found that people with a history of drug problems almost always chose benzos over a dummy pill, but they were tested in other labs' studies, mostly at much bigger doses, so it can't be told whether their history made the difference. Moderate drinkers chose diazepam more often than light drinkers, and anxious people chose benzos when they could take capsules as they felt they needed them. Outside labs, some people report getting high: the review cites a US school survey in which about half of students who used tranquilizers without a prescription said they usually got high, and in a 2015–16 US survey 12 in 100 adults who misused benzos named getting high as their main reason.

risk_of_bias.note: The claim is about which people choose benzodiazepines, a comparison between kinds of people. The contrast between people with and without histories of problem drug use is made across separate studies, by different laboratories, mostly at very different doses and with different procedures, so dose and procedure could explain it; the review reports that choice depended on dose but does not discuss this. The review's selection is unsystematic (card sc_griffiths_1997: high), 11 of its 13 drug-history studies are the first author's, and several of its labels rest on its own one-tailed re-tests. Within de Wit et al. (1986) anxious and non-anxious volunteers were compared at the same doses (RoB 2 some concerns on card sc_de_wit_1986: allocation to orders not described, staff blinding not stated, completers only, mood results tabulated only where significant).

inconsistency.note: Within each kind of person the direction is consistent: volunteers without problem drug use did not choose a benzodiazepine over placebo in any of the single-dose or capsule-by-capsule studies tabulated for them, and people with problem drug use chose it in every placebo-controlled study tabulated for them. indirectness.note: Apart from de Wit et al. (1986), the evidence is second-hand, through one narrative review whose primary papers were not read. imprecision.note: 2 to 16 people per study among people with problem drug use and about 10 to 14 per group in most other studies; the comparisons between kinds of people are small (de Wit et al.: 11 to 13 per group, no difference detected; anxious against other volunteers 65% against 45%, P = 0.06; moderate against light drinkers significant in one study of 27 people); no pooled estimate or interval.

grade.reasoning: Rated as observational because the claim is about who chooses benzodiazepines, a comparison between kinds of people made mostly across separate studies (METHODS 6.3; brief for this round), although each study's own comparison of the drug with a placebo is within-person and mostly double-blind. Low start; risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 give very low (the scale stops there). The within-person finding of de Wit et al. (1986) alone, that 36 volunteers without problem drug use, anxious or not, mostly chose a placebo over single morning doses of diazepam, which calmed and sedated them without raising euphoria scores, rests on a counterbalanced, placebo-controlled comparison and a behavioural outcome and would be moderate on its own (high start; imprecision −1: 36 people, no intervals); the same laboratory found the same in other volunteers, as the review summarizes, which is replication by the same team. The contrast with people with problem drug use rests on the review's comparison of separate studies by another laboratory, mostly at much higher doses, and cannot separate history from dose; the statement says so and does not give it as the review's own caution, which it is not. Status replicated by the same team: volunteers without problem drug use were studied mainly by the Chicago group (de Wit, Johanson, Uhlenhuth) and people with problem drug use mainly by the review's first author's group, and no study read compared the two at the same doses. Choosing a drug over a placebo is not the same as feeling high: the review's definition of reinforcement covers any motive, and only de Wit et al. measured euphoria directly. The school-survey figure is second-hand and the national survey figure qualifies the claim without being part of the rating. The review's findings on how fast the drug acts and its comparisons of benzodiazepines by appeal are left out by design. Doses are given only as study conditions; nothing here is advice on amounts or use.

statement: Among US civilian adults living in households in 2015 and 2016, past-year misuse of benzodiazepines (any use other than as a doctor directed, by self-report) was reported by 2.2% (95% CI 2.0 to 2.3), against 10.4% (10.1 to 10.7) who reported using them only as prescribed; the people reporting misuse most often gave relaxing or relieving tension (47.1%) or help with sleep (26.6%) as their main reason, and getting high less often (11.6%), and most often got the pills from a friend or relative (68.8% in all, editors' sum). Certainty: low. Status: single study. The figures come from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), a national probability survey answered by computer, partly in a private audio-assisted section meant to encourage honest answers, in 86,186 adults (Maust et al., 2019). In all, 12.6% (12.2 to 12.9) reported past-year benzodiazepine use, an estimated 30.6 million adults a year, so misuse made up 17.2% of use (5.3 million people against 25.3 million). Misuse counted taking a benzodiazepine without a prescription and taking one's own in greater amounts, more often or for longer than prescribed, and anyone reporting any misuse in the past year counted as misusing even if they also took it as prescribed. It was most common at ages 18 to 25 (5.2% of all adults that age; 51.0% of their benzodiazepine use) and least common at 65 or older (0.6%). Of the 2,533 people reporting misuse, 73.9% had taken a benzodiazepine without a prescription; the one misused was most often alprazolam (Xanax; 75.1%), then diazepam (20.5%), clonazepam (20.0%) and lorazepam (15.4%), some people naming more than one. Their main reasons, from a list: to relax or relieve tension 47.1%, to help with sleep 26.6%, to get high 11.6%, to help with feelings or emotions 10.1%, to experiment 6.0%, to increase or decrease the effects of another drug 1.6%, and 'hooked or have to have it' 0.6%. These shares add to 103.6% (editors' sum; 104.0% at ages 18 to 49 and 101.3% at 50 or older), more than rounding can explain, and 'another reason', also on the list, is not shown; the paper does not say whether people could give more than one main reason, so the shares cannot be read as exactly one reason per person. Getting high was the main reason for 13.9% at ages 18 to 49 and 3.0% at 50 or older, and sleep for 22.4% and 41.7%. Sources: free from a friend or relative 53.2%, bought from one 12.3% and stolen from one 3.3%, one doctor 19.5%, two or more doctors 0.9%, bought from a dealer or stranger 7.7%, and stolen from a health care setting 0.1% (together 97.0%, editors' sum; the rest not shown). Of the people reporting misuse, 4.6% (3.7 to 5.6) met DSM-IV criteria for past-year abuse and 6.8% (5.6 to 8.2) for past-year dependence, and they reported a mean of 5.4 days of misuse in the past month (whether people with no misuse that month are counted is not stated). Among people who used benzodiazepines, misuse rather than use as prescribed went with younger age, being male, and use, misuse or use disorders of alcohol, marijuana, prescription opioids and prescription stimulants, a cross-sectional association that shows nothing about cause. All of it is self-report without checks; adults in institutions and on active military duty are not covered; response rates are not given; and the 2015 redesign of the survey means the figures cannot be compared with earlier years. The authors suggest that part of what the survey counts as misuse may be people treating anxiety or insomnia that has gone untreated because of poor access to care; the analysis did not test this.
plain: Why do people misuse benzos like Xanax? In a big US survey in 2015 and 2016, about 13 in 100 adults said they had taken a benzodiazepine in the past year, and about 2 in 100 said they had misused one, meaning any use a doctor did not direct, such as taking pills without a prescription (the most common kind) or taking more of their own than prescribed. Three in four of the people who misused one had misused alprazolam (Xanax). Asked for their main reason, 47 in 100 said to relax or relieve tension, 27 in 100 to sleep, 12 in 100 to get high and 10 in 100 to cope with feelings; these shares add up to a little over 100, and the paper does not explain why. About 69 in 100 got the pills from a friend or relative, mostly for free. About 7 in 100 of the people who misused benzos met the criteria for dependence. These are people's own answers, not checked, and the survey did not include people living in institutions, such as prisons, or on active military duty.

evidence.extracted: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2015 and 2016 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH): a 50-state multistage area probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population, administered by RTI International for SAMHSA, answered in two computer-assisted parts, one private and audio-assisted to encourage honest reporting of illicit drug use; 86,186 adults. Benzodiazepine use counted when named in the tranquilizer (anxiety or muscle spasm) and sedative (insomnia) items (10,290 people; details in an online supplement). Since the 2015 redesign misuse means any use other than as a doctor directed: without a prescription, in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed, or in any other way; anyone reporting any past-year misuse counts as misusing, even if they also used the drug as prescribed. People reporting misuse were asked its manner, their reasons (to relax, to experiment, to get high, for sleep, for emotions, to counter the effect of another drug, because they were hooked, or another reason) and the source; abuse and dependence by DSM-IV criteria.
